templates.name: Main purpose: literary reaction, mood or trait
Function: example or supporting detail for a claim
Main purpose: profile of a person, work or institution
Three moves: introduces a researcher, describes an aspect of the work, explains its significance
Function: set-up or context for what follows
Describes how a discovery was made, then explains its importance
Presents a philosophy or set of principles, then describes a work shaped by it
Describes a problem in research on a topic, then sketches a researcher’s approach to it
The speaker addresses a criticism of himself, then declares an ambition or commitment (poem)
Function: qualification of an earlier description
Introduces a person, then gives characteristics of their work

items.passage: Red knots (Calidris canutus) breed in the high Arctic, where warming has advanced the date of snowmelt, and overwinter along the coast of Mauritania. Analyzing 33 years of morphological measurements, Jan van Gils and colleagues determined that knots hatched in early-snowmelt summers matured into smaller adults with shorter bills. In Mauritania, these short-billed individuals consumed fewer of the deeply buried bivalves that constitute their principal prey, depended more heavily on seagrass rhizomes, and exhibited lower survival rates.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes research showing that red knots have come to rely on seagrass in Mauritania because the bivalves they once ate there have grown scarce.
It presents research linking conditions where a bird species breeds to how well the birds fare in a distant wintering region.
It explains how researchers used decades of measurements to show that red knots with shorter bills find more food in years when Arctic snow melts early.
It discusses a long-term study in order to argue that the main threat to red knots is a loss of seagrass along the coast of Mauritania.
items.explanation: The text explains that red knots hatched in Arctic summers with early snowmelt grow up smaller and with shorter bills, and that in Mauritania, where the birds spend the winter, these short-billed knots eat fewer buried bivalves and survive at lower rates. It therefore presents research tying a change in the birds’ breeding grounds to how well they fare in a distant wintering region, as choice B states.

A.why_wrong: The text does say short-billed knots relied more on seagrass, but it explains this by their bills: they ate fewer bivalves because the prey is deeply buried. The text gives no sign that the bivalves have grown scarce.

C.why_wrong: The decades of measurements are real, but the text links shorter bills to eating fewer bivalves and surviving at lower rates, not to finding more food.

D.why_wrong: The text reports findings rather than arguing about threats, and seagrass is what the short-billed birds turned to, so nothing in the text suggests it is disappearing.

sources.what: van Gils et al. 2016, Science, abstract: red knots breeding in the warming high Arctic produce smaller offspring with shorter bills in summers with early snowmelt; at the tropical wintering grounds (Mauritania) shorter-billed individuals have reduced survival, associated with eating fewer deeply buried bivalves and more seagrass rhizomes (33 years of body-size data, per the paper)

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology). Key B. Band 6 hard P_study: the key is a two-step paraphrase (Arctic snowmelt shapes body size; body size shapes survival in Mauritania) with no knot, bill or snow wording. A and C keep true details (seagrass; decades of measurements) and fail on a cause or result the text states; D flips a neutral report into an argument and misreads the seagrass. The abstract calls the link an association, so the passage reports the pattern without claiming the decline of the species is caused by it. Own blind solve: B.

review.note: blind solve contaminated: key seen while inspecting the file layout; core claim confirmed from the abstract via the Europe PMC REST API (the cited page returns 403 to fetch)

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Tobias Smollett’s 1771 novel The Expedition of Humphry Clinker. Jery Melford, who is traveling with his uncle, writes to a friend.

The truth is, [my uncle’s] disposition and mine, which, like oil and vinegar, repelled one another at first, have now begun to mix by dint of being beat up together. I was once apt to believe him a complete Cynic; and that nothing but the necessity of his occasions [needs] could compel him to get within the pale of society—I am now of another opinion. I think his peevishness arises partly from bodily pain, and partly from a natural excess of mental sensibility.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It records a change in how the narrator regards his uncle, ending with the conclusion that the uncle shuns company out of contempt for other people.
It describes how the narrator and his uncle, once alike in temperament, have grown apart since the narrator began observing the uncle closely.
It presents a reassessment in which the narrator comes to view his uncle’s irritable nature more sympathetically than he once did.
It recounts how the narrator’s temperament has gradually blended with his uncle’s, a change that has led the narrator to share the uncle’s scorn for society.
items.explanation: Jery says he once thought his uncle “a complete Cynic” who joined society only when he had to, but that he is “now of another opinion”: he now traces the uncle’s “peevishness” to “bodily pain” and “a natural excess of mental sensibility,” a far kinder account than the charge of cynicism. The text thus presents a reassessment in which Jery views his uncle’s irritability more sympathetically, as choice C states.

A.recipe: first clause right, later clause gives the rejected view (REV)
A.why_wrong: The text does record a change in Jery’s view, but contempt for others is the opinion he gives up (“I was once apt to believe him a complete Cynic … I am now of another opinion”), not the one he reaches.

B.recipe: word hook on the oil-and-vinegar image, reversed (LIT/REV)
B.why_wrong: The image says the two were unlike at first and have now begun to “mix,” the reverse of being alike and growing apart.

D.recipe: first clause right (the temperaments mixing), later clause invented (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text does say the two temperaments have begun to “mix,” but Jery never says he has come to share any scorn for society; he gives up the very view that his uncle is a scornful “Cynic.”

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Humphry Clinker, J. Melford to Sir Watkin Phillips, Hot Well, April 18); novel first published 1771

items.notes: Area: literature (epistolary novel, 1771, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #2160, Jery Melford’s letter dated Hot Well, April 18, second paragraph from “The truth is”; CB-style adaptation, hence “adapted from”: “his” replaced by the gloss “[my uncle’s]”, the gloss “[needs]” after “occasions”, the double hyphen printed as a closed em dash, and the letter’s sentence ended at “sensibility” (its closing clause on the mind’s “morbid excess of sensation” cut for length). Context line matches the source: Jery writes to his college friend Sir Watkin Phillips and travels with his uncle Matthew Bramble (and other relatives). Key C. Band 7 P_lit modeled on b0f7541b (3.3) without its first-impression-reversed frame: the key hinges on the two-part cause. Section 6 checks: key 21 words, options 21 to 26 words (mean 23.5); key parts 2 (revised view; two-part cause); A and D keep a true first clause and fail later on stated text. Passage 110 words incl. attribution against the model’s 122. Own blind solve: C. Reviewer: key C and option D rewritten (see review); key now 21 words, options 21 to 26.
band7_moves: dual purpose key: the narrator’s revised view and its two-part explanation
two distractors keep a true first clause (A: a change in view; D: a judgment about the cause) and fail on stated text
B literalizes and reverses the oil-and-vinegar image

fixes: key C rewritten as an abstract reassessment ('view his uncle’s irritable nature more sympathetically') instead of a paraphrase of the last sentence
D replaced: the absolute 'entirely' died to 'partly ... partly'; new D keeps the true first clause (the temperaments mixing) and invents the later one (shares the uncle’s scorn)
review.note: excerpt checked against Gutenberg #2160: exact apart from the glosses, the closed em dash and the closing clause cut after 'sensibility'; CB adapted items cut closing clauses the same way: ea971260 (Alcott, after a semicolon, as here), 6557f7fc (Wharton), c228bd45 (Nesbit), 659c6c1d (Stevenson), b0f7541b (Melville, mid-sentence with a bracketed bridge), so 'adapted from' and the cut are accepted

band7.why: After hardening. As written it read band 6: D’s 'entirely' died to 'partly ... partly' and the key paraphrased the last sentence. Now: 1771 prose; the key is an abstract reassessment sharing no passage wording and needs two linked steps (the opinion changed; pain and sensitivity are a kinder cause than cynicism); A and D keep a true first clause (a change of view; the temperaments mixing) and fail only later; B reverses the oil-and-vinegar image.

items.passage: Rufino Tamayo repudiated the principle, championed by the muralists who dominated Mexican art after the Revolution, that modern Mexican painting must advance an explicitly political program, and many in the nation’s artistic establishment regarded his independence as bordering on betrayal. Yet his art was no less grounded in Mexico than theirs. <u>As head of ethnographic drawing at the National Museum of Archaeology in Mexico City during the 1920s, Tamayo worked daily among pre-Hispanic sculpture and vernacular crafts</u>, a tradition he would later identify as the source of his work.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It supports the claim in the previous sentence by describing how Tamayo became immersed in the traditions that informed his art.
It explains how Tamayo’s work at the museum led him to reject the political program that, according to the first sentence, the muralists upheld.
It describes the museum job that, according to the first sentence, caused Mexico’s arts establishment to regard Tamayo as close to a traitor.
It offers an example of the muralists’ influence on Tamayo’s early career, an influence that the rest of the sentence suggests he later rejected.
items.explanation: The previous sentence claims that Tamayo’s art was “no less grounded in Mexico” than the muralists’ art. The underlined portion supports that claim by describing his daily work among pre-Hispanic sculpture and folk art, a tradition that, the rest of the sentence adds, he later called the source of his work.

B.why_wrong: The text ties the museum work to the sources of Tamayo’s art, not to his break with the muralists; the first sentence presents that break as a matter of principle about political art.

C.why_wrong: According to the first sentence, the establishment objected to Tamayo’s “independence” from the political program, and that sentence never mentions his museum job.

D.why_wrong: The museum brought Tamayo into contact with pre-Hispanic and folk art, not with the muralists, and the rest of the sentence says he embraced that tradition as the source of his work.

sources.what: Tamayo refused the rule that modern Mexican art must serve an overtly socialist agenda; seen by the arts establishment as bordering on treason; at the National Museum he came into contact with pre-Hispanic and popular arts and called that tradition the source of his work

items.notes: Area: humanities (painting). Key A. Band 6 hard F_example: the span supports a claim stated in the previous sentence; the key paraphrases “grounded in Mexico” as “traditions that informed his art.” Built unlike 3.10 (Cruse’s position): the key names a support relation, not a position. B, C and D each start from a true link to the first sentence (his rejection of the program; the establishment’s view; the muralists) and fail on what the text states. Britannica (via search) gives his post as head of the department of ethnographic drawing, National Museum of Archaeology, 1921 to 1926. Own blind solve: A.

review.note: core claim confirmed on The Art Story (rejected overt revolutionary content, seen as bordering on treason, worked in the Department of Ethnographic Drawing, called the tradition the source of his work)

items.passage: Hisako Koyama began observing sunspots in 1944 through a refracting telescope from her father, and in 1946 she became a staff observer at the institution in Tokyo now called the National Museum of Nature and Science, where she observed with a single instrument throughout her tenure. Across more than four decades she produced over 10,000 meticulous drawings of the solar disk. Solar physicists reconstructing sunspot counts back to 1610 have designated her records one of the project’s “backbones,” bridging a gap between early twentieth-century observations and those of the space age.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe Koyama’s drawings and explain why they replaced earlier records as the basis for counts of sunspots going back to 1610
To recount how Koyama became interested in the Sun and show that her drawings were valued chiefly for their artistry
To describe a reconstruction of sunspot counts since 1610 and identify the space-age instruments on which it chiefly depends
To describe an observer’s long career and explain why scientists rely on her records to reconstruct a historical series
items.explanation: The text describes Koyama’s decades of sunspot observation, which produced more than 10,000 drawings made with a single telescope, and then explains that solar physicists use her records as a “backbone” of a reconstruction of sunspot counts back to 1610 because they bridge a gap between other sets of observations. Choice D captures both parts.

A.why_wrong: Koyama’s records bridge a gap between early twentieth-century and space-age observations, so they join those records rather than replacing them.

B.why_wrong: The text does say how Koyama began, with her father’s telescope, but it says scientists value her drawings as data for sunspot counts, not for their artistry.

C.why_wrong: The reconstruction is mentioned to show why Koyama’s records matter; the text names no space-age instruments, and its subject throughout is Koyama.

sources.what: AGU press release on Knipp, Liu and Hayakawa 2017 (Space Weather): Koyama began observing in spring 1944 with a refracting telescope from her father; staff observer at the National Museum of Nature and Science from 1946; same telescope throughout her tenure; more than 10,000 drawings over more than 40 years; her records are one of the backbones of the sunspot number reconstruction back to 1610, bridging a gap between early 20th-century and space-age records

items.notes: Area: science history (astronomy). Key D. Band 6 hard P_profile on the model of 3.18 (describe X and explain Y): D is a two-part abstract summary; A keeps D’s frame and reverses the bridging relation; B and C each fit one sentence only. The museum was then the Tokyo Science Museum, hence “the museum in Tokyo now called.” Own blind solve: D.

review.note: AGU release unreachable (DNS); same release read on colorado.edu (1944 start, father’s refractor, staff from 1946, same telescope, over 10,000 drawings, 'backbones', bridging gap, back to 1610)
review.safety_note: safety solve: 'the same instrument' read as her father's telescope; now 'a single instrument', as the source says

items.passage: It has long been asserted that cheetahs abandon chases because they overheat, but the evidence behind that claim is thinner than its popularity suggests: it derives largely from a 1973 experiment in which two hand-reared cheetahs, lifelong captives, were run on a laboratory treadmill. When Robyn Hetem and colleagues implanted sensors in cheetahs hunting at a rehabilitation park, the animals’ body temperatures barely rose during chases, successful or not. The largest increases occurred after kills, possibly reflecting stress, the team suggests, since a fresh carcass can attract lions and hyenas.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It discusses a 1973 experiment and a later study of hunting cheetahs to show that the instruments used in the earlier experiment gave inaccurate temperature readings.
It presents a study of cheetahs hunting on their own to suggest that a widely repeated explanation of their behavior rests on unrepresentative evidence.
It reports a study of cheetahs’ body temperatures to show that stress over guarding a kill, not the strain of running, is what makes cheetahs abandon chases.
It uses a study of hunting cheetahs to argue that laboratory experiments on animals generally give a misleading picture of how animals behave in the wild.
items.explanation: The text says the evidence that cheetahs end chases because they overheat is “thinner than its popularity suggests,” since it comes mostly from two lifelong captives run on a treadmill. It then describes a study of cheetahs hunting for themselves whose temperatures barely rose during chases. The study is thus presented to suggest that a popular explanation rests on evidence that does not reflect real hunting, as choice B states.

A.recipe: first clause right, invented reason for doubt (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text does discuss both studies, but it doubts the 1973 evidence because it came from two lifelong captives run on a treadmill, not because of faulty instruments; it never questions the earlier measurements themselves.

C.recipe: first clause right, findings blended into an invented cause (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text links the largest temperature rises to the period after kills, when stress may play a part, but it never says what makes cheetahs abandon chases, and a chase that ends in a kill has not been abandoned.

D.why_wrong: The text casts doubt on one claim that rests on one treadmill experiment; it draws no conclusion about laboratory experiments on animals in general.

sources.what: Hetem et al. 2013 (National Geographic report): the overheating idea traces to a 1973 treadmill study of a couple of hand-reared cheetahs captive all their lives; sensors implanted in cheetahs at a rehabilitation park; body temperature barely rose while sprinting, in successful and unsuccessful hunts; larger rises in the 40 minutes after kills, which Hetem attributes to stress because lions and hyenas can take a carcass

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal physiology). Key B. Band 7 P_view on the model of c61a7c4a (3.4): an earlier finding generalized from artificial conditions, then field data that do not bear it out, with the evaluative marker in the first sentence; the frame differs from w2b2_05 and w2b3_05 (popular beliefs about behavior). Section 6 checks: key 24 words; options 24 to 28 words (mean 25.5); key parts 2 (the study; what it suggests about the old claim); all three distractors keep the study and fail on stated text. The source calls the overheating idea a myth, so “thinner than its popularity suggests” does not overstate it. Own blind solve: B. Reviewer: options A and C rewritten (see review); options now 24 to 27 words.
band7_moves: hedged dual purpose: the study and what it suggests about a long-repeated claim
all three distractors keep a true first clause (the studies) and change the result or the purpose
abstract key: no cheetah, treadmill or temperature wording
evaluative marker in the first sentence, as in c61a7c4a

fixes: A replaced: 'stop running at about the same body temperature' died to 'barely rose'; new A keeps both studies and invents a reason for doubt (faulty instruments)
C replaced: 'successful hunts, unlike unsuccessful ones' died to 'successful or not'; new C blends the after-kill stress finding into a false cause of abandoned chases
review.note: core claim confirmed on National Geographic (two hand-reared lifelong captives on a 1973 treadmill; six cheetahs at a rehabilitation park; temperatures barely rose in successful and failed hunts; larger rise after kills, stress, lions and hyenas)

band7.why: After hardening. Hedged dual purpose (a study, used to suggest the old evidence is unrepresentative); all three distractors keep the study and fail in a later clause: A an invented reason for doubting the 1973 data, C a false cause built from the after-kill finding, D an overreach to all laboratory work. Before, A and C each died to one stated fact.

items.passage: Excluded, as German women then were, from university study, Agnes Pockels began investigating the surfaces of liquids at home in the 1880s, after observing how soap affected dishwater. She devised a trough with a sliding barrier for quantifying how contaminants such as soap alter the surface tension of water. Lord Rayleigh forwarded her account of the results to Nature, which published it in 1891, and Irving Langmuir subsequently refined her design: the Langmuir–Blodgett trough, still used to characterize thin molecular films, descends directly from her apparatus.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a self-taught scientist, outlines the instrument she devised, and then explains why established researchers long ignored the findings she reported.
It introduces an amateur investigator, credits a famous physicist with designing her apparatus, and then describes how she improved it over many years.
It introduces a researcher without formal training, describes an apparatus she created, and then traces that apparatus’s influence on later science.
It describes an observation made during household work, explains how a physicist tested it, and then reports the conclusions he published in 1891.
items.explanation: The text first introduces Pockels, who could not attend a university and worked at home; it then describes the sliding-barrier trough she devised; finally it explains that Langmuir built on her design and that an instrument still in use descends from it. Choice C follows these three moves in order.

A.recipe: first two moves right, third reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: Far from being ignored, Pockels’s results were forwarded to Nature by Rayleigh, published in 1891, and built on by Langmuir.

B.recipe: first move right, later moves misattributed (SWAP)
B.why_wrong: Pockels devised the trough herself; Rayleigh forwarded her account, and it was Langmuir, not Pockels, who later worked with an improved version.

D.recipe: first move right, later moves misattributed (SWAP)
D.why_wrong: Pockels, not a physicist, carried out the measurements; Rayleigh only forwarded her account, which Nature published as hers.

sources.what: Agnes Pockels: women barred from universities; interest from dishwashing and soap; devised a slide trough for quantitative measurements of surface properties; Rayleigh forwarded her findings to Nature (1891); Langmuir used an improved version; her device is a direct antecedent of the Langmuir–Blodgett trough

items.notes: Area: science history (physical chemistry). Key C. Band 6 hard S13 on the model of 3.6 (introduces a researcher, describes the work, shows why it mattered). Hard pattern: A keeps moves 1 and 2 and breaks move 3 by stance; B and D keep move 1 and misassign the later moves to Rayleigh, each ruled out by a stated fact. Options vary their wording for the shared moves so no three share a long prefix. Own blind solve: C.

review.note: core claim confirmed on Wikipedia (barred from university, dishwashing, slide trough, Rayleigh to Nature 1891, Langmuir’s improved trough, direct antecedent of the Langmuir–Blodgett trough)

items.passage: Because horses at Botai, a settlement in northern Kazakhstan occupied about 5,500 years ago, wore bits and harnesses and the community’s pottery retained mares’ milk residues, <u>Botai has frequently been identified as the place where today’s domestic horses originated</u>. Genomic analysis by Charleen Gaunitz and colleagues complicates that interpretation: the Botai horses gave rise not to modern domestic breeds but to Przewalski’s horses, which the team concluded are feral descendants of herded animals rather than, as long believed, the last wild horses.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It presents an inference from archaeological finds that, the text explains, genetic analysis has narrowed by showing that only certain modern breeds descend from the Botai horses.
It states a view based on finds at Botai that the text later rejects on the grounds that the Botai horses were wild animals that had never been herded.
It identifies the evidence that led researchers to sequence ancient horse genomes, a project that the text says was designed to find the wild ancestors of Przewalski’s horses.
It presents a conclusion drawn from archaeological evidence that, according to the text, genetic findings about the Botai horses’ descendants have since called into doubt.
items.explanation: The underlined portion states a common view, based on the bits, harnesses and mares’ milk found at Botai, that today’s domestic horses originated there. The next sentence says genomic analysis “complicates that interpretation,” because the Botai horses gave rise to Przewalski’s horses rather than to modern domestic breeds. Choice D describes both the basis of the view and how the text goes on to undercut it.

A.recipe: first part right, outcome narrowed instead of overturned (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text does not say that some modern breeds descend from the Botai horses: it says the Botai horses gave rise “not to modern domestic breeds but to Przewalski’s horses.”

B.recipe: first part right, wrong reason (INV ruled out by the text)
B.why_wrong: The text says Przewalski’s horses descend from herded animals, so it does not claim the Botai horses were never herded; it complicates the view because of whose ancestors those horses were.

C.recipe: wrong label for the span, invented aim (REL/INV)
C.why_wrong: The underlined portion is the view itself; the evidence for it (bits, harnesses, milk residues) comes earlier in the sentence, and the text names no aim of finding the ancestors of Przewalski’s horses.

sources.what: Gaunitz et al. 2018 (Science), as reported by Sci.News: Botai horses wore bits and were harnessed, and mares’ milk residues were found in Botai pottery; Przewalski’s horses are the feral descendants of horses herded by the Botai, not truly wild; Botai horses did not give rise to modern domestic horses

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology (genetics). Key D. Band 7 F_setup on the model of 1f2d6173 and a2f64e58: the span is a view that a later sentence complicates, and the key carries both halves. Section 6 checks: key 25 words; options 25 to 29 words (mean 27); key parts 2 (a conclusion drawn from archaeological evidence; doubted by genetic findings); A and B keep a true first clause and fail later on stated text; the span is a means, and the deciding clue comes after it. The paper finds only about 2.7 percent Botai ancestry in domestic horses of the last 4,000 years, so “complicates” is used rather than “refutes”; the date of about 5,500 years is the usual dating of the Botai culture (secondary detail). Own blind solve: D. Reviewer: option A and the last clause of the passage rewritten (see review).
band7_moves: span is a view the next sentence complicates; the key carries both halves
two distractors keep a true first clause (A, B) and fail on stated text
B uses the “last truly wild horses” detail as a trap that the text itself answers (feral descendants of herded animals)
abstract key: no horse, bit or milk wording; “the Botai horses’ descendants” is the only named element

fixes: passage: 'now recognized as feral descendants' (stronger than the source) changed to the team’s conclusion
A hardened from a straight reversal that mirrored the key ('later supported') to a near miss ('narrowed ... only certain modern breeds')
review.note: core claim confirmed on Sci.News (bits and harness, mares’ milk in pottery, Botai did not give rise to today’s horses, Przewalski’s horses feral descendants of Botai herds)

band7.why: The span is a means (a view a later sentence overturns) and the key carries both halves, depending on the sentence after the span; A (hardened from a mirror reversal to 'narrowed ... only certain breeds') and B keep the first half and fail later; B needs the chain Przewalski’s horses, descended from Botai herds, so herded; key shares almost no passage wording.

items.passage:
The following text is from H. G. Wells’s 1910 novel The History of Mr. Polly.

[Mr. Polly] suffered from indigestion now nearly every afternoon in his life, but as he lacked introspection he projected the associated discomfort upon the world. Every afternoon he discovered afresh that life as a whole and every aspect of life that presented itself was “beastly.” And this afternoon, lured by the delusive blueness of a sky that was blue because the wind was in the east, he had come out in the hope of snatching something of the joyousness of spring. The mysterious alchemy of mind and body refused, however, to permit any joyousness whatever in the spring.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To portray a character who blames the world for a discomfort that actually comes from his own body
To suggest that a character’s gloom is caused mainly by the cold east wind that blows in early spring
To describe a character’s delight in the arrival of spring after a long and difficult winter
To explain why a character has begun taking walks each afternoon in order to improve his health
items.explanation: The text says that Mr. Polly, who suffers from indigestion nearly every afternoon, “projected the associated discomfort upon the world,” so that every afternoon he finds life “beastly.” Even his outing in search of spring’s joy fails because of “the mysterious alchemy of mind and body.” The text thus portrays a man who blames the world for a discomfort that comes from his own body.

B.recipe: word hook on the east wind (LIT)
B.why_wrong: The east wind is mentioned only as the reason the sky looked deceptively blue; the text traces Mr. Polly’s mood to his indigestion and “the mysterious alchemy of mind and body.”

C.why_wrong: Mr. Polly went out hoping to enjoy the spring, but the text says his condition would not “permit any joyousness whatever.”

D.why_wrong: He went out “in the hope of snatching something of the joyousness of spring,” not for his health, and the text describes only this one afternoon’s outing.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (The History of Mr. Polly, chapter 1, section I); novel first published 1910

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1910, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #7308, chapter 1, section I, third paragraph; the opening “He” replaced by the gloss “[Mr. Polly]”. No context line: the excerpt itself establishes the situation. Key A paraphrases “projected the associated discomfort upon the world.” Own blind solve: A.

review.note: excerpt exact against Gutenberg #7308 apart from '[Mr. Polly]' for 'He'; CB uses 'is from' for the same pronoun gloss (9aa44886, Gatsby)

items.passage: Poachers remove sea turtle eggs from nesting beaches throughout Central America, but once the eggs leave the sand, investigators rarely discover their destinations. <u>To follow them, Helen Pheasey and colleagues placed 3D-printed decoy eggs containing GPS transmitters in 101 turtle nests on four beaches in Costa Rica.</u> About a quarter of the decoys were taken. Most remained fairly close to where they had been placed, but one traveled 137 kilometers, passing through a supermarket’s loading bay before reaching a residence, and so revealed an entire trafficking chain.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents a hypothesis about where stolen eggs are sold that the following sentences go on to disprove.
It points out a weakness of the decoys that, according to the following sentence, limited the study’s results.
It describes the method the researchers used to address the problem identified in the previous sentence.
It summarizes the main finding of the study, which the rest of the text then explains in greater detail.
items.explanation: The previous sentence identifies a problem: once turtle eggs are taken, investigators rarely discover where they end up. The underlined sentence describes how the researchers tackled it, by hiding GPS-equipped decoy eggs in nests, and the remaining sentences report what the decoys revealed.

A.why_wrong: The sentence proposes no hypothesis; it describes what the researchers did, and the following sentences report the results of doing it.

B.why_wrong: The sentence names no weakness of the decoys, and the following sentences describe what the decoys successfully revealed.

D.why_wrong: The findings (how many decoys were taken and where they went) come after the underlined sentence, which describes the method rather than any result.

sources.what: Pheasey et al. 2020, Current Biology, abstract: the InvestEGGator, a 3D-printed decoy turtle egg with a GPS-GSM transmitter, placed in clutches to track trafficked sea turtle eggs; the most detailed track identified an entire trade chain covering 137 km (101 nests on four Costa Rican beaches, about a quarter taken, most staying local: University of Kent release)

The following text is from John Greenleaf Whittier’s 1847 poem “Proem.”

Nor mine the seer-like power to show
The secrets of the heart and mind;
To drop the plummet-line below
Our common world of joy and woe,
A more intense despair or brighter hope to find.

Yet here at least an earnest sense
Of human right and weal [well-being] is shown;
A hate of tyranny intense,
And hearty in its vehemence,
As if my brother’s pain and sorrow were my own.

O Freedom! if to me belong
Nor mighty Milton’s gift divine,
Nor Marvell’s wit and graceful song,
Still with a love as deep and strong
As theirs, I lay, like them, my best gifts on thy shrine.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

The speaker admits the limits of his talent as a poet, then pledges his poetry to a cause he cares about deeply.
items.explanation: The speaker says he lacks the “seer-like power” to reveal “the secrets of the heart and mind” and lacks Milton’s and Marvell’s gifts; yet his poems show “an earnest sense / Of human right” and a hatred of tyranny, and he lays his “best gifts” on Freedom’s shrine. He thus admits his limits and then dedicates his poetry to a cause, as choice D states.

A.why_wrong: The speaker answers no critics, and far from ranking himself with Milton he says that Milton’s “gift divine” does not belong to him.

B.why_wrong: He says his poems show feeling “As if my brother’s pain and sorrow were my own,” so he does not regret being unable to share others’ suffering.

C.recipe: first move partly right, second reversed (REV)
C.why_wrong: He does mention Milton’s and Marvell’s gifts, but he offers his own “best gifts,” his poems, to Freedom; he has not given up poetry.

items.passage: In the centuries before 1000 CE, the island of Helgö, in a lake in eastern Sweden, was a flourishing center of commerce and metalworking with connections extending to distant regions. Among the artifacts recovered there is <u>a bronze statuette of the Buddha, probably manufactured in the late 400s or early 500s in the Swat Valley, in present-day Pakistan</u>. Archaeologists excavating the site also uncovered a bishop’s staff from Ireland and a bronze vessel from Egypt.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why metalworkers on the island made statues of the Buddha.
It describes how the island’s trade with Ireland and Egypt began.
It shows that the island had become an important center of Buddhist worship in Sweden.
It gives one piece of evidence that the island had links to faraway places.
items.explanation: The first sentence says Helgö had “connections extending to distant regions.” The underlined portion gives evidence of those connections: a statuette of the Buddha made thousands of kilometers away, in the Swat Valley. The final sentence adds more such objects.

A.why_wrong: The statuette was probably made in the Swat Valley, not by metalworkers on Helgö.

B.why_wrong: Ireland and Egypt come up only in the final sentence, which lists other objects found at the site; the text says nothing about how that trade began.

C.why_wrong: One statuette shows a connection to a distant place; the text says nothing about Buddhist worship on the island.

items.passage: Many picture books for young children depict animals wearing clothes and talking like people. Psychologist Patricia Ganea and her colleagues investigated whether such books influence what children learn about real animals. They read three- to five-year-olds a book about an unfamiliar animal; some children heard it described in factual language, while others heard it described as talking and having humanlike intentions. Children of every age in the second group were afterward more likely to attribute human characteristics to real animals, even though the book’s pictures had been realistic.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It explains why authors of children’s picture books often show animals wearing clothes.
It describes a study of how one feature of children’s books affects what young readers learn.
It argues that preschoolers should not be allowed to read books in which animals talk.
It compares how children and adults respond to books about animals they have never seen.
items.explanation: The text describes research on whether books that present animals as humanlike change what children learn: some children heard a factual description of an animal and others a humanlike one, and the second group more often attributed human characteristics to real animals. Choice B states this purpose.

A.why_wrong: The text notes that such books are common but gives no reason why authors write them.

C.why_wrong: The text reports findings; it makes no recommendation about what preschoolers should read.

D.why_wrong: The study involved only three- to five-year-olds; no adults took part.

items.passage: When water runs short, plants compete for it, yet some trees supply water to their neighbors. In a 1993 study, ecologist Todd Dawson found that sugar maples perform <u>what scientists call “hydraulic lift”</u> during droughts. At night, the trees’ deep roots absorb groundwater from saturated soil far below the surface, and their shallow roots release some of it into the parched upper layers. Every neighboring plant Dawson examined consumed some of this redistributed water, and those that depended on it most grew more vigorously than plants that used little or none.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a term for a process that the following sentence explains.
It presents a hypothesis that Dawson’s results went on to disprove.
It describes a problem that sugar maples cause for the plants around them.
It explains why Dawson chose to study sugar maples rather than other trees.
items.explanation: The underlined portion gives the name scientists use, “hydraulic lift,” and the next sentence explains the process: deep roots take up water at night and shallow roots release some of it into the parched upper soil. Choice A describes this function.

B.why_wrong: The underlined portion names a process Dawson found, and the rest of the text describes it; nothing is disproved.

C.why_wrong: The text says neighboring plants consumed the lifted water and grew more vigorously, so the maples help rather than harm them.

D.why_wrong: The text does not say why Dawson chose sugar maples.

items.notes: Area: natural science (plant ecology). Key A. Easy F_term on the model of 1.11, built differently: the term arrives inside a research finding in sentence 2, and the explanation follows. Own blind solve: A.
